facts.text: In Italy the film is Dèmoni 2: L'incubo ritorna. West Germany knew it as Dance of the Demons 2, or Dämonen 2, when it opened there on July 9, 1987.
Demons 2 started shooting on May 19, 1986, just seven months after the first Demons hit Italian theaters. Producer Dario Argento and director Lamberto Bava wasted no time on the sequel.
The security guard at the desk is played by Lino Salemme, who also appeared in the first Demons. Several faces from that film came back in new roles.
Nancy Brilli (Hannah) isn't a horror fan. She took the job anyway because she wanted to work with special effects.
Bobby Rhodes played the pimp Tony in the first Demons. Here he returns as a different character, gym instructor Hank, a bodybuilder rather than a pimp.
Coralina Cataldi-Tassoni plays Sally Day. In the first Demons, the blind man's niece Liz was played by an actress named Sally Day. It's an in-joke between the two films.
Asia Argento (Ingrid) made her feature film debut here at age 10. She is the daughter of producer Dario Argento, and later starred in xXx and Land of the Dead.
Demons 2 was first meant to follow the survivor of the original film. That actor declined to return, so Dario Argento and Lamberto Bava built an all-new apartment-block story.
Goof: when the phone rings at Sally's party, the receiver is on backwards, which would stop it from ringing. It's also put back on backwards after the call.
Effects wizard Sergio Stivaletti sat in on the script sessions. He ended up credited as a writer alongside Dario Argento, Lamberto Bava, Franco Ferrini and Dardano Sacchetti.
The demon's revival was made by filming a melting wax head and then running the footage in reverse.
Composer Simon Boswell wanted The Smiths' 'Panic' for the film. He told Morrissey it was a drama about passive TV consumption, hiding the gore. The Smiths later said yes.
The demon coming out of the TV was done with an actor in a mask pressing his face against a latex screen. Low-tech and effective.
Fangoria's Blu-ray review points out this demon climbing out of a TV set came years before Sadako in Ringu. Ringu (1998) is among the films that reference Demons 2.
Continuity goof: the birthday cake on screen now doesn't match the one seen at the start. The hand-lettering is different, and Sally's candles change length between shots.
The Smiths' 'Panic' was recorded in May 1986, the month this film started shooting. It was released as a single that July and hit No. 11 in the UK.
Demons 2 swaps the first film's heavy metal for British goth and new wave: The Smiths, The Cult, Dead Can Dance, Love and Rockets, Gene Loves Jezebel and more. Simon Boswell chose them.
Argento's usual band Goblin was too busy to score this one. Simon Boswell stepped in and steered the producer away from prog rock and metal toward bands Boswell loved.
Composer Simon Boswell hadn't seen the first Demons when he scored the sequel. His earlier work for the Argento family was the score for Dario Argento's Phenomena.
Reviewer Angel Orona on the Grindhouse Database compared the film to Cronenberg's Shivers, then called it apples-and-oranges. He recommended it as a 'backdrop movie' for a party.
Demons 2 was reportedly the first film to get an X rating from the MPAA without sex or nudity. The transformation sequences were judged too intense for an R.
Asia Argento wasn't the first Argento kid in the series. Her older sister Fiore Argento had a supporting role in the first Demons.
Director Lamberto Bava says producer Dario Argento visited the set often but never gave direction: 'he fully respected my role as the director.'
Sergio Stivaletti's animatronic demon was nicknamed Menelik. Some said it copied Gremlins. Stivaletti denied it, citing Bosch's painting Triptych of the Temptation of St. Anthony.
Goof: a male gym member with a line earlier vanishes from the garage battle after about 54 minutes, and nobody notices he's gone.
The film's visible grain isn't only age. Synapse's release notes say the negative stock used on Demons 2 was weaker than the original film's.
Bava and Argento toned down the gore to get an Italian V.M.14 rating, yet the film still got an X in the US. The demons ooze green fluid rather than blood.
Demons 2 was shot in Hamburg, Germany and Rome, at De Paolis studios. It cost about $1.5 million and earned roughly 1.1 billion lire in Italy.
The German release lost over 9 minutes to avoid a ban like the first film's, and its ending was nearly removed. A US release on VHS and DVD is about 3 minutes longer than the R-rated cut.
Slant Magazine's Budd Wilkins said the sequel trades gore for 'surreal shocks and quasi-Cronenbergian craziness.' AllMovie praised only Sergio Stivaletti's effects. Rotten Tomatoes sits at 73%.
A planned Demons 3 would have trapped plane passengers on a volcanic island. The writers abandoned it, and a church-set script became Michele Soavi's The Church (1989).
Lamberto Bava finally wrote a sequel in 2025: the novel Demoni 3: La rinascita, in which the demons spread through social media instead of television.
Plot hole: George and Hannah took a class on rappelling out of a burning building. No other tenant seems to have taken it.
In the original script, Hannah's baby would have turned into a demon and clawed out of her. Lamberto Bava and Dario Argento chose a happier ending.
Demons 2 opened in Italy on October 9, 1986, in the US on February 13, 1987, and in the UK that September.
Director Lamberto Bava is the son of Italian horror master Mario Bava. He began as his father's assistant director before directing Macabre (1980).
Dread Central's Matt Serafini called Demons 2 a mixed bag. He still wondered why it never became a series, and wanted new Italian filmmakers to revive it with practical effects and new wave music.
